rv.q: I feared the worst, not least because Snook is a woman and Dorian Gray isn’t. But how much better she turns out to be than some fashionable male twerp starlet with cheekbones. Snook is far from snookered by Wilde’s twisted, camp, gothic horror novel.

That’s because she and they are the cast in this sizzlingly clever adaptation of Oscar Wilde’s novel. Director Kip Williams, of Sydney Theatre Company, has the super-smart idea of packaging Wilde’s Gothic classic for our own age — a world obsessed with image where you can curate your life, your likes and your looks on the smartphone in your hand.
Sarah Snook triumphs in this game-changing piece of theatre
Snook...embodies them all with absolute and unflagging conviction
This is raw, human misery, only heightened by the artifice that surrounds it.
Snook is an absolute marvel...Everything is an illusion, except for Snook
Her timing is perfect; she has to perform in real time and react to pre-recorded footage, all the while jumping between the role of narrator and every character.
This 'Picture of Dorian Gray' is, on its own terms, a triumph.

cn.t: Critics praise Sarah Snook's virtuosic performance embodying every character with conviction, though some question whether the production's technical wizardry overshadows the story itself.
